findings.title: A timed-out waiter moved to another bucket leaves its entry behind
findings.scenario: Scenarios 3 and 4, contract cases F07 and F09
findings.summary: futex_wait_bitset saves its bucket reference from the original key (futex.rs:79), and after pause_timeout it removes its FutexItem only from that bucket (futex.rs:124). A cross-bucket REQUEUE moves the item into another bucket (futex.rs:513-534), so a waiter that times out after the move, or after observing expiry but before cleanup, misses the lookup and returns 0 instead of ETIMEDOUT (futex.rs:125-130). Dropping the Waiter closes the waker, and the closed item stays in the global destination bucket for good: WAKE retains it because wake_up returns false, and both migration paths still count it. The 56-state MC_hunt_s3_owner counterexample violates ResourceAccountingBalance. The 93-state MC_hunt_s4_live_migration counterexample (spec/output/hunt-round2/MC_hunt_s4_live_migration-bfs.out) shows the Linux-visible consequence, LiveMigrationExhaustion: a later REQUEUE(1,1) from that key moves the dead entry and leaves a live waiter behind. Implementation traces case-11 and case-13 show the same histories on SMP=2. Linux follows q->lock_ptr in futex_unqueue (core.c:921-964), so a completed waiter never stays queued. Each stranded item retains an Arc<Waker> and its Arc<Task>, including an exited thread's kernel stack. That growth is inferred from the code and was not measured.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 3 (moved wait completes through its saved original cleanup bucket — same stale-original-bucket mechanism at futex.rs:79-124 and 500-533) and code-review Scenario 4 (retained closed entry consumes a later live migration's quota — the LiveMigrationExhaustion consequence shown by the MC_hunt_s4_live_migration counterexample), as well as the brief's §6.3 code-review-only finding (the original-bucket-miss claim at futex.rs:124-129 overlooks cross-bucket requeue), which the brief itself routes into the MC-1 audit.

findings.title: Ordinary REQUEUE with a zero wake quota wakes a waiter
findings.summary: sys_futex converts FUTEX_REQUEUE's wake count with futex_val_to_max_count, which raises 0 to 1 (syscall/futex.rs:106,146-151). That at-least-one rule belongs to Linux FUTEX_WAKE only (waitwake.c:192). Linux REQUEUE uses nr_wake unchanged and tests the quota before each waiter (requeue.c:585,607), so REQUEUE(0,0) wakes nothing. In the 20-state counterexample, REQUEUE(A to B, 0, 0) accepts and removes one of two enrolled waiters. MC_hunt_s2_quotas.cfg fails the same clause on the same-bucket path. Implementation trace case-16 woke one waiter and returned 1 for REQUEUE(0,0). The Linux 7.2.8 control returned 0 and left both waiters on the source key.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 2's zero-wake-quota divergence, the brief's test-verifiable lead TV-1 (REQUEUE wake zero becomes one, syscall/futex.rs:105-109,146-150).

findings.title: A same-bucket REQUEUE with a zero migration quota moves one waiter
findings.summary: update_item_keys rekeys a matching entry and counts it before testing count >= max_count (futex.rs:500-511). With a migration quota of 0, the first remaining entry moves whenever it matches the source key. The cross-bucket path tests the quota first (futex.rs:522-523), and Linux tests task_count - nr_wake >= nr_requeue before each waiter (requeue.c:585). In the 22-state counterexample, REQUEUE(A to C, 1, 0), with A and C sharing a bucket, wakes one waiter and moves the other to C. A later WAKE on A then misses it. Implementation trace case-05 shows this, and cases 06 and 07 (different buckets, unrelated first entry) move nothing. The Linux 7.2.8 control moved no waiter for REQUEUE(1,0).
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 2's same-bucket zero-migration divergence, the brief's test-verifiable lead TV-2 (same-bucket migration zero can move the first remaining entry, futex.rs:500-511).

findings.title: REQUEUE returns only the number of woken waiters
findings.scenario: Scenario 2, contract cases F03 and F06 (TV-3)
findings.summary: futex_requeue returns Ok(nwakes) (futex.rs:381), the requeue helpers report no count, and identical addresses take the futex_wake shortcut (futex.rs:353-355). Linux ordinary REQUEUE counts every woken or requeued waiter, including same-address requeues (requeue.c:607-610,691). In the 30-state counterexample, REQUEUE(A to B, 1, 1) wakes one waiter, moves the other and returns 1 instead of 2. MC_hunt_s2_same_address.cfg (24 states, spec/output/hunt-round2/MC_hunt_s2_same_address-bfs.out) fails the same invariant for identical addresses. Implementation traces case-03, case-04 and case-09 returned 1. The Linux 7.2.8 control returned 2 in both shapes. The FUTEX_REQUEUE manual page describes only woken waiters, which conflicts with the pinned source and the running kernel.
findings.dedup_note: also covers code-review Scenario 2's return-count and same-address divergence, the brief's test-verifiable lead TV-3 (return counts only accepted wakes and the same-address shortcut omits processed requeues, futex.rs:353-354,381).

findings.title: A user value update and WAKE can overlap WAIT registration, including the unlocked fault-retry window
findings.summary: Code-review Scenario 1 hypothesizes that a user value store and FUTEX_WAKE can overlap futex_wait_bitset's atomic load, comparison and enqueue, including the window where a recoverable fault unlocks the bucket, resolves the page, reacquires the lock and repeats the locked load (kernel/core/src/process/posix_thread/futex.rs:79-119, thread_local.rs:102-135). The current implementation holds the bucket across load, compare and enqueue, matching Linux's locked reload (waitwake.c:591-663), and the ostd Waiter preserves pending wakes between enqueue and actual parking (ostd/src/sync/wait.rs:192-201,262-275), so the brief asserts no new lost-registration defect; the open question is whether the atomic comparison/registration contract can still let a wait miss a required wake. Model checking found no violation for this mechanism: MC_hunt_s1_registration.cfg (BFS, 289 states, diameter 31) held NoMissedOrderedWake including the unlock/fault/relock/reload path, and MC_hunt_s1_mismatch.cfg (BFS, 31 states, plus a 30-minute simulation covering 9,759,957 states) confirmed that a mismatching EAGAIN leaves no registration. It therefore enters confirmation as a mechanism hypothesis without a counterexample, not as a confirmed bug. Historical issues #981 and #2306 (the repaired non-atomic read and fault-in-atomic-mode paths) are context for this scenario, not rediscovery targets.
findings.dedup_note: Not represented by any MC finding: the Scenario 1 hunting configs ran clean, so this is the only code-review scenario emitted as a separate candidate.
